claims.claim: Acutely, taVNS increased heart rate, blood pressure, and peripheral perfusion index without affecting the corrected QT interval, ICP, or HRV.
claims.source: Acutely, taVNS increased heart rate, blood pressure, and peripheral perfusion index without affecting the corrected QT interval, ICP, or HRV.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the acute cardiovascular measurements taken before, during, and after taVNS treatment.

claims.claim: The acute post-treatment elevation in heart rate was more pronounced in patients who experienced a decrease of more than one point in their modified Rankin Score at the time of discharge.
claims.source: The acute post-treatment elevation in heart rate was more pronounced in patients who experienced a decrease of more than one point in their modified Rankin Score at the time of discharge.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis between heart rate changes and clinical outcomes.

claims.claim: taVNS treatment did not induce adverse cardiovascular effects, such as bradycardia or QT prolongation.
claims.source: Our study found that taVNS treatment did not induce adverse cardiovascular effects, such as bradycardia or QT prolongation, supporting its development as a safe immunomodulatory treatment approach for SAH patients.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the cardiovascular monitoring data collected throughout the study.

claims.claim: The observed acute increase in heart rate after taVNS treatment may serve as a biomarker for SAH patients who could derive greater benefit from this treatment.
claims.source: The observed acute increase in heart rate after taVNS treatment may serve as a biomarker for SAH patients who could derive greater benefit from this treatment.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed correlation between heart rate changes and clinical outcomes.

claims.claim: SAH represents a significant global health burden and causes permanent disability in approximately 30% of survivors.
claims.source: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is a devastating subtype of stroke that represents a significant global health burden and causes permanent disability in approximately 30% of survivors (D'Souza, 2015; Weir, 2002; Zhang et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on SAH outcomes.

claims.claim: Early brain injury can occur within the first 24–48 hr after ictus, which involves a cascade of elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) and a subsequent drop of cerebral perfusion.
claims.source: Early brain injury can occur within the first 24–48 hr after ictus, which involves a cascade of elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) and a subsequent drop of cerebral perfusion (Schneider et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on early brain injury after SAH.

claims.claim: Systemic and local inflammation, cerebral edema, blood–brain barrier disruption, sympathetic nervous system activation, autoregulatory failure, microthrombosis, spreading depolarizations, and inflammation have all been observed during the early brain injury period.
claims.source: Systemic and local inflammation, cerebral edema, blood–brain barrier disruption, sympathetic nervous system activation, autoregulatory failure, microthrombosis, spreading depolarizations, and inflammation have all been observed during this period (Macdonald et al., 2012; Budohoski et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the pathophysiology of early brain injury.

claims.claim: Delayed cerebral ischemia typically occurs between 5 and 14 days after the SAH.
claims.source: These biological processes result in the inability of cerebral perfusion to match metabolic demands, leading to secondary brain injury and delayed cerebral ischemia that typically occurs between 5 and 14 days after the SAH (Provencio, 2013; van Gijn et al., 2007; Tracey, 2002; Lv et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the timing of delayed cerebral ischemia.

claims.claim: Delayed cerebral ischemia and deleterious inflammation are major predictors of poor outcomes and morbidity.
claims.source: Delayed cerebral ischemia and deleterious inflammation are major predictors of poor outcomes and morbidity.
claims.evidence: This claim draws from established medical knowledge about SAH outcomes.

claims.claim: SAH is believed to cause sympathetic predominance, which plays a key role in the development of cerebral vasospasm.
claims.source: SAH is believed to cause sympathetic predominance, which plays a key role in the development of cerebral vasospasm, renders patients more susceptible to non-neurological complications, and exacerbates deleterious inflammatory processes (Naredi et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on autonomic dysfunction after SAH.

claims.claim: Recent studies have demonstrated taVNS efficacy in reducing inflammation, improving autonomic balance, and enhancing brain plasticity.
claims.source: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) is one of the most promising therapeutic options, as recent studies have demonstrated its efficacy in reducing inflammation, improving autonomic balance, and enhancing brain plasticity (Wu et al., 2023; Bonaz et al., 2016; Meyers et al., 2018; Provencio and Vora, 2005; Huguenard et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on taVNS effects.

claims.claim: Stimulating the auricular branch of the vagus nerve has been shown to activate the same brain regions as cervical vagus nerve stimulation.
claims.source: Stimulating the auricular branch of the vagus nerve has been shown to activate the same brain regions as cervical vagus nerve stimulation (Frangos et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on the neural effects of auricular stimulation.

claims.claim: taVNS mediates cholinergic signaling and regulates pro-inflammatory responses via the inflammatory reflex.
claims.source: Specifically, taVNS mediates cholinergic signaling and regulates pro-inflammatory responses via the inflammatory reflex (Figure 1A; Sahn et al., 2023; Pavlov and Tracey, 2012)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: In the inflammatory reflex, inflammatory mediators such as cytokines trigger afferent vagus nerve signaling, which then prompts an efferent response that acts to reduce the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
claims.source: In this reflex, inflammatory mediators such as cytokines trigger afferent vagus nerve signaling. This afferent signal then prompts an efferent response from the vagus nerve that acts to reduce the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Tynan et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on the inflammatory reflex mechanism.

claims.claim: Two reviews of human studies have considered the cardiovascular effects of taVNS generally safe, with adverse effects reported only in patients with pre-existing heart diseases.
claims.source: While some animal studies have reported a potential risk of bradycardia and decreased blood pressure associated with vagus nerve stimulation, two reviews of human studies have considered the cardiovascular effects of taVNS generally safe, with adverse effects reported only in patients with pre-existing heart diseases (Naggar et al., 2014; Hua et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles on taVNS safety.

claims.claim: Cardiovascular abnormalities following SAH, such as prolonged elevated heart rate and QT prolongation, are associated with an increased risk of poor outcomes.
claims.source: This is particularly notable as cardiovascular abnormalities following SAH, such as prolonged elevated heart rate and QT prolongation, are associated with an increased risk of poor outcomes (Norberg et al., 2018; Schmidt et al., 2014; Zhang and Qi, 2016; van der Bilt et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on cardiovascular complications after SAH.

claims.claim: Based on a meta-analysis, most aversive effects of taVNS were seen in repeated sessions lasting 60 min or more.
claims.source: Based on a meta-analysis, most aversive effects were seen in repeated sessions lasting 60 min or more; therefore, we hypothesized that repetitive taVNS increased HRV but did not cause bradycardia and QT prolongation (Kim et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis on taVNS effects.

claims.claim: RMSSD indicates parasympathetic activity, while lower SDNN is associated with increased cardiac risk.
claims.source: RMSSD indicates parasympathetic activity, while lower SDNN is associated with increased cardiac risk (Kleiger et al., 2005; Shaffer and Ginsberg, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on HRV metrics.

claims.claim: Twenty-four participants were randomized to receive the taVNS (N = 11) or Sham (N = 13) treatment.
claims.source: Twenty-four participants were randomized to receive the taVNS (N = 11) or Sham (N = 13) treatment (Table 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the study data presented in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The participants, the medical team who dictated all management decisions for the patient's SAH, and the outcomes assessors who assigned mRS at admission and discharge were blinded to the treatment.
claims.source: The participants, the medical team who dictated all management decisions for the patient's SAH, and the outcomes assessors who assigned mRS at admission and discharge were blinded to the treatment.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the study design and blinding procedures.

claims.claim: Enrolled patients underwent 20 min of either taVNS or sham stimulation twice daily during their stay in the ICU.
claims.source: Following randomization, enrolled patients underwent 20 min of either taVNS or sham stimulation twice daily during their stay in the ICU.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the treatment protocol used in the study.

claims.claim: For taVNS treatments, ear clips were placed along the concha of the ear, while for sham treatments, the clips were placed along the earlobe.
claims.source: For taVNS treatments, these ear clips were placed along the concha of the ear, while for sham treatments, the clips were placed along the earlobe to avoid stimulation of the auricular vagus nerve from tactile pressure (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the treatment protocol, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: For the taVNS group, stimulation parameters were 20 Hz frequency, 250 µs pulse width, and 0.4 mA intensity.
claims.source: For the taVNS group, stimulation parameters were selected based on values reported in prior studies that sought to maximize vagus somatosensory evoked potentials while avoiding the perception of pain: 20 Hz frequency, 250 µs pulse width, and 0.4 mA intensity (de Gurtubay et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the treatment parameters, supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The stimulation parameters were designed to be imperceptible to the patients, and there were no reports of detection of taVNS.
claims.source: The stimulation parameters were designed to be imperceptible to the patients, and there were no reports of detection of taVNS, suggesting the success of the blinding.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the study outcomes related to blinding success.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in heart rate between groups (Mann–Whitney U test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, p-value = 0.69, Cohen's d = −0.01, W-statistics = 4317, power = 0.93).
claims.source: We found no significant differences in heart rate between groups (Figure 2D, Mann–Whitney U test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, p-value = 0.69, Cohen's d = −0.01, W-statistics = 4317, power = 0.93).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of heart rate data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Changes in heart rate from Day 1 were equivalent between groups (two-tailed equivalence tests, p[lower threshold] = 0.006, test statistics[lower threshold] = 2.53; p[lower threshold] = 0.004, test statistics[lower threshold] = −2.72, N(VNS) = 94, N(VNS) = 95).
claims.source: Changes in heart rate from Day 1 were equivalent between groups (two-tailed equivalence tests, p[lower threshold] = 0.006, test statistics[lower threshold] = 2.53; p[lower threshold] = 0.004, test statistics[lower threshold] = −2.72, N(VNS) = 94, N(VNS) = 95).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by equivalence testing of heart rate changes.

claims.claim: Changes in corrected QT interval from Day 1 were significantly higher in the Sham group compared to the taVNS group (Mann–Whitney U test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, p-value <0.001, Cohen's d = −0.57).
claims.source: Moreover, changes in corrected QT interval from Day 1 were significantly higher in the Sham group compared to the taVNS group (Figure 2E, Mann–Whitney U test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, p-value <0.001, Cohen's d = −0.57).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of QT interval data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: After the phase of early brain injury, the mean and median corrected QT interval were lower in the taVNS group with large effect sizes (|Cohen's d| >0.5).
claims.source: After the phase of early brain injury, the mean and median corrected QT interval were lower in the taVNS group with large effect sizes (Figure 2E, |Cohen's d| >0.5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by effect size analysis of QT interval data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Changes in prolonged QT intervals percentage from Day 1 were higher in the Sham group (Mann–Whitney U test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, p-value <0.001, Cohen's d = −0.72).
claims.source: We found that changes in prolonged QT intervals percentage from Day 1 were higher in the Sham group (Figure 2F, Mann–Whitney U test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, p-value <0.001, Cohen's d = −0.72).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of prolonged QT interval data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Changes in SDNN using Day 1 as baseline were not significantly different between the treatment groups (T-test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, p = 0.479, Cohen's d = 0.10, t statistics = 0.71).
claims.source: We found that changes in SDNN using Day 1 as baseline were not significantly different between the treatment groups (T-test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, p = 0.479, Cohen's d = 0.10, t statistics = 0.71, Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of SDNN data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Changes in RMSSD using Day 1 as baseline were significantly higher in the taVNS treatment group (T-test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.025, Cohen's d = 0.42, t statistics = 2.91).
claims.source: Changes in RMSSD using Day 1 as baseline were significantly higher in the taVNS treatment group (T-test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.025, Cohen's d = 0.42, t statistics = 2.91, Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of RMSSD data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The taVNS treatment increased RMSSD over the course of the treatment, with a smaller effect size (Cohen's d = 0.29) observed between Days 2 and 4, and large effect sizes at the later phases (Cohen's d = 0.41 for Days 5–7, Cohen's d = 0.54 for Days 8–10, Cohen's d = 0.66 for Days 11–13).
claims.source: The taVNS treatment increased RMSSD over the course of the treatment, with a smaller effect size (Cohen's d = 0.29) observed between Days 2 and 4, corresponding to the early brain injury phase, and large effect sizes at the later phases (Cohen's d = 0.41 for Days 5–7, Cohen's d = 0.54 for Days 8–10, Cohen's d = 0.66 for Days 11–13).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by effect size analysis of RMSSD data at different time points.

claims.claim: Overall HRV change from Day 1 was significantly higher in the VNS group (Mann–Whitney U test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, p-value = 0.04, Cohen's d = 0.37).
claims.source: Overall HRV change from Day 1 was significantly higher in the VNS group (Figure 3E, Mann–Whitney U test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, p-value = 0.04, Cohen's d = 0.37).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of overall HRV factor scores shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The parasympathetic activity was significantly higher in the VNS treatment group, with the largest effect size between Days 2 and 4 (Cohen's d = 0.50).
claims.source: The parasympathetic activity was also significantly higher in the VNS treatment group, and we observed the largest effect size between Days 2 and 4 (Cohen's d = 0.50, Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of parasympathetic activity factor scores shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Heart rate was lower in patients with improved mRS (Mann–Whitney U test, N(mRS < 0) = 122, N(mRS > 0) = 98, p-value <0.01, Cohen's d = −0.54).
claims.source: We found that heart rate was lower in patients with improved mRS (i.e., <0) (Mann–Whitney U test, N(mRS < 0) = 122, N(mRS > 0) = 98, p-value <0.01, Cohen's d = −0.54).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis correlating heart rate with clinical outcomes.

claims.claim: No significant differences were detected in changes in blood pressure and ICP between the treatment groups.
claims.source: No significant differences were detected in changes in blood pressure and ICP between the treatment groups (Figure 4B, C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of blood pressure and ICP data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claims.claim: Equivalence testing confirmed that the ICP changes from the first hospitalization day were not significantly different between treatment groups, with a 2-mmHg equivalence margin.
claims.source: Equivalence testing confirmed that the ICP changes from the first hospitalization day were not significantly different between treatment groups, with a 2-mmHg equivalence margin (two one-sided t-tests, p[lower threshold] = 3.66 × 10−13, t[lower threshold] = 8.07; p[upper threshold] = 3.33 × 10−10, t[upper threshold] = −6.73).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by equivalence testing of ICP data.

claims.claim: PPI change was significantly lower in the taVNS group (Mann–Whitney U test, N(taVNS) = 83, N(Sham) = 95, Bonferroni corrected p < 0.01, Cohen's d = −0.49).
claims.source: We found that PPI change was significantly lower (Mann–Whitney U test, N(taVNS) = 83, N(Sham) = 95, Bonferroni corrected p < 0.01, Cohen's d = −0.49).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of PPI data.

claims.claim: Respiration rate change was significantly higher in the taVNS group, as compared to the Sham group (Mann–Whitney U test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, Bonferroni corrected p = 0.02, Cohen's d = 0.37).
claims.source: In addition, respiration rate change was significantly higher (Mann–Whitney U test, N(taVNS) = 94, N(Sham) = 95, Bonferroni corrected p = 0.02, Cohen's d = 0.37) in the taVNS group, as compared to the Sham group (Figure 4D, E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of respiration rate data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claims.claim: There was a significant negative correlation between changes in PPI and changes in respiration rate only for the taVNS treatment group (Pearson correlation coefficient = −0.37, p < 0.001).
claims.source: We found a significant negative correlation between changes in PPI and changes in respiration rate only for the taVNS treatment group (Pearson correlation coefficient = −0.37, p < 0.001, t-test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The changes in heart rate were not significantly different between treatment groups although heart rate increased in the taVNS group (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, N = 188, Bonferroni corrected p = 0.03, Cohen's d = 0.11) but not in the Sham group (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, N = 199, Bonferroni corrected p = 0.72, Cohen's d = 0.00).
claims.source: We found that the changes in heart rate were not significantly different between treatment groups although heart rate increased in the taVNS group (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, N = 188, Bonferroni corrected p = 0.03, Cohen's d = 0.11) but not in the Sham group (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, N = 199, Bonferroni corrected p = 0.72, Cohen's d = 0.00) (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of acute heart rate changes shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The increase in heart rate after taVNS was within 0.5 standard deviations of daily heart rate.
claims.source: However, the increase in heart rate after taVNS was within 0.5 standard deviations of daily heart rate.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the magnitude of heart rate changes relative to daily variability.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in changes in corrected QT interval or HRV, as measured by RMSSD, SDNN, and relative power of high-frequency band between treatment groups.
claims.source: There were no significant differences in changes in corrected QT interval or HRV, as measured by RMSSD, SDNN, and relative power of high-frequency band between treatment groups (Figure 5D, E, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of acute cardiovascular changes shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: The slope between changes in heart rate and changes in mRS is significantly more negative for the taVNS treatment group.
claims.source: Our analysis revealed that the slope between changes in heart rate and changes in mRS is significantly more negative for the taVNS treatment group (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by linear mixed-effects model analysis shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: An increase in heart rate following acute taVNS treatment is associated with improved clinical outcomes.
claims.source: This finding suggests that an increase in heart rate following acute taVNS treatment is associated with improved clinical outcomes (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Patients in the taVNS treatment group who had an improvement in mRS of –2 or greater compared to other patients had significantly greater increases in heart rate (Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.02, N(mRS change < −1) = 53, N(mRS change ≥ −1) = 135, Cohen's d = 0.34).
claims.source: Post hoc analysis showed that patients in the taVNS treatment group who had an improvement in mRS of –2 or greater compared to other patients had significantly greater increases in heart rate (Mann–Whitney U test, p = 0.02, N(mRS change < −1) = 53, N(mRS change ≥ −1) = 135, Cohen's d = 0.34, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Changes in PPI and blood pressure were significantly higher in the taVNS group, as compared to the Sham group (Mann–Whitney U test, blood pressure: p = 0.03, Cohen's d = 0.22, N = 180 for Sham and 159 for taVNS; PPI: p < 0.01, Cohen's d = 0.19, N = 227 for Sham and 186 for taVNS).
claims.source: We found that changes in PPI and blood pressure were significantly higher in the taVNS group, as compared to the Sham group (Mann–Whitney U test, blood pressure: p = 0.03, Cohen's d = 0.22, N = 180 for Sham and 159 for taVNS; PPI: p < 0.01, Cohen's d = 0.19, N = 227 for Sham and 186 for taVNS, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of acute PPI and blood pressure changes shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Only PPI remained significantly different between treatment groups after Bonferroni correction.
claims.source: Only PPI remained significantly different between treatment groups after Bonferroni correction.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the statistical significance after multiple comparison correction.

claims.claim: The acute changes in PPI and blood pressure remained within the daily standard deviation.
claims.source: The acute changes in PPI and blood pressure remained within the daily standard deviation.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the magnitude of acute changes relative to daily variability.

claims.claim: No significant differences in post-treatment changes in ICP or respiration rate were observed between treatment groups.
claims.source: No significant differences in post-treatment changes in ICP or respiration rate were observed between treatment groups.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of acute ICP and respiration rate changes.

claims.claim: Repetitive taVNS is not associated with previously suggested risks, such as bradycardia and QT prolongation.
claims.source: The findings in our study indicate that repetitive taVNS is not associated with previously suggested risks, such as bradycardia and QT prolongation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cardiovascular monitoring data collected throughout the study.

claims.claim: Repetitive taVNS treatment increased overall HRV and parasympathetic activity, which are indicators of a healthy cardiovascular system.
claims.source: Furthermore, repetitive taVNS treatment increased overall HRV and parasympathetic activity, which are indicators of a healthy cardiovascular system.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the HRV analysis and draws from established knowledge about HRV as a health indicator.

claims.claim: taVNS only significantly increased the PPI but not heart rate, HRV, corrected QT interval, blood pressure, or ICP when looking at the acute effects.
claims.source: When looking at the acute effects, taVNS only significantly increased the PPI but not heart rate, HRV, corrected QT interval, blood pressure, or ICP.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the acute cardiovascular effects based on the statistical analyses.

claims.claim: Heart rate can serve as a biomarker for identifying SAH patients who are most likely to benefit from taVNS treatment.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that heart rate can serve as a biomarker for identifying SAH patients who are most likely to benefit from taVNS treatment.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation between heart rate changes and clinical outcomes.

claims.claim: This study substantiates the safety of treating SAH patients with taVNS and provides foundational data for future efforts to optimize and translate taVNS therapy toward clinical use.
claims.source: Collectively, this study substantiates the safety of treating SAH patients with taVNS and provides foundational data for future efforts to optimize and translate taVNS therapy toward clinical use.
claims.evidence: This is a concluding statement about the implications of the study findings.

claims.claim: The autonomic balance is shifted toward sympathetic dominance following SAH.
claims.source: Our study is aligned with the finding that the autonomic balance is shifted toward sympathetic dominance following SAH (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Chiu et al., 2012; Bai et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the study data shown in figures and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Dysregulation of sympathovagal balance toward sympathetic dominance could be restored by taVNS treatment.
claims.source: In addition, we found that dysregulation of sympathovagal balance toward sympathetic dominance could be restored by taVNS treatment.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the HRV analysis showing increased parasympathetic activity with taVNS.

claims.claim: The parasympathetic activity was significantly higher in the taVNS treatment group, with this difference most pronounced during the early phase, between Days 2 and 4 following SAH.
claims.source: Specifically, factor analysis based on HRV metrics showed that the parasympathetic activity was significantly higher in the taVNS treatment group. This difference was most pronounced during the early phase, between Days 2 and 4 following SAH.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the factor analysis of HRV metrics.

claims.claim: The relative power of the high-frequency band is widely used to indicate respiratory sinus arrhythmia, a process primarily driven by the parasympathetic nervous system.
claims.source: The relative power of the high-frequency band (0.15–0.4 Hz)—to validate the accuracy of the factor analysis. The relative power of the high-frequency band is widely used to indicate respiratory sinus arrhythmia, a process primarily driven by the parasympathetic nervous system.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge regarding HRV frequency-domain measures.

claims.claim: Both the change in parasympathetic activity factor and relative high-frequency power were higher in the taVNS group at the early phase (Days 2–4).
claims.source: We found that both the change in parasympathetic activity factor and relative high-frequency power were higher in the taVNS group at the early phase (Days 2–4, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Higher high-frequency power was observed in the Sham group during the later phase.
claims.source: Conversely, we observed higher high-frequency power in the Sham group during the later phase.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the HRV analysis at different time points.

claims.claim: The respiration rate was higher in the taVNS treatment group, a compensatory mechanism to ensure oxygen delivery.
claims.source: Given that the respiration rate was higher in the taVNS treatment group, a compensatory mechanism to ensure oxygen delivery (Figure 4E), we hypothesized that the observed lower high-frequency power in the taVNS treatment group compared to sham at later phases was a result of increased respiration rate.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed increase in respiration rate shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The normalized high-frequency power was higher when RR was less than 25 bpm compared to when RR >25 bpm (Cohen's d = 0.85).
claims.source: Indeed, we found the normalized high-frequency power was higher when RR was less than 25 bpm compared to when RR >25 bpm (Cohen's d = 0.85, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: An increase in RR in the taVNS treatment group was associated with a decrease in high-frequency power.
claims.source: Moreover, an increase in RR in the taVNS treatment group was associated with a decrease in high-frequency power (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: taVNS led to a decreased QTc without a significant change in heart rate, mimicking the effects observed with propranolol administration.
claims.source: Additionally, taVNS led to a decreased QTc without a significant change in heart rate, mimicking the effects observed with propranolol administration, a beta-blocker that reduces sympathetic activity (Solti et al., 1989).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the QTc and heart rate data and draws a comparison to the effects of propranolol, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Repetitive taVNS reduces sympathetic overactivation and influences ventricular repolarization processes.
claims.source: This finding suggests that repetitive taVNS reduces sympathetic overactivation and influences ventricular repolarization processes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in QTc.

claims.claim: Age was negatively correlated with changes in heart rate, SDNN, and RMSSD from Day 1 but not with changes in QT intervals.
claims.source: This analysis showed that age was negatively correlated with changes in heart rate, SDNN, and RMSSD from Day 1 but not with changes in QT intervals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ANCOVA analysis with age as a covariate.

claims.claim: After adjusting for age, RMSSD and SDNN changes were significantly higher, while QTc changes were significantly lower in the taVNS treatment group.
claims.source: After adjusting for age, we found that RMSSD and SDNN changes were significantly higher, while QTc changes were significantly lower in the taVNS treatment group (Appendix 4—table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ANCOVA analysis shown in Appendix 4—table 1.

claims.claim: Lower RMSSD and SDNN in older individuals suggest a greater shift toward sympathetic predominance following SAH.
claims.source: Specifically, lower RMSSD and SDNN in older individuals suggest a greater shift toward sympathetic predominance following SAH (Appendix 4—table 1).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the age-related differences in HRV metrics shown in Appendix 4—table 1.

claims.claim: PPI is primarily influenced by cardiac output and vascular tone.
claims.source: PPI is primarily influenced by cardiac output and vascular tone.

results.result: This randomized clinical trial enrolled 24 SAH patients (11 taVNS, 13 sham) with appropriate blinding of participants, medical team, and outcome assessors. The treatment protocol involved 20-minute sessions of taVNS (20 Hz, 250 µs, 0.4 mA) or sham stimulation twice daily during ICU stay.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C27-C32, C118-C123 collectively describe the study design, randomization, blinding procedures, and treatment parameters. The methodology is clearly documented with appropriate ethical approval, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and blinding procedures that support the validity of the trial design.

results.result: Repetitive taVNS did not significantly alter heart rate, blood pressure, or intracranial pressure compared to sham treatment over the course of hospitalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C33-C34, C44-C45, C89 demonstrate through statistical testing (Mann-Whitney U tests, equivalence tests) that repetitive taVNS did not cause significant changes in these cardiovascular parameters. The high statistical power (0.93 for heart rate) and equivalence testing strengthen these null findings.

results.result: Repetitive taVNS reduced QT interval prolongation compared to sham treatment, with significantly lower corrected QT intervals and percentage of prolonged QT intervals in the taVNS group after the early brain injury phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37, C59, C73-C74 show statistically significant reductions in QTc changes (p<0.001, Cohen's d=-0.57) and prolonged QT percentage (p<0.001, Cohen's d=-0.72) in the taVNS group. The effect mimics propranolol administration, suggesting reduced sympathetic overactivation.

results.result: Repetitive taVNS significantly increased heart rate variability (HRV) and parasympathetic activity compared to sham treatment, with the largest effect on parasympathetic activity observed during Days 2-4 (Cohen's d=0.50).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C39-C42, C60, C65-C66, C91, C116 demonstrate through multiple HRV metrics (RMSSD, overall HRV factor, parasympathetic activity factor) that taVNS increased parasympathetic tone. The factor analysis approach (C141-C147) provides robust evidence by isolating parasympathetic activity from confounding factors like respiration rate.

results.result: The increase in parasympathetic activity from taVNS was most pronounced during the early brain injury phase (Days 2-4), potentially mitigating sympathetic overactivation before the typical onset of cerebral vasospasm.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C66, C68, C95 show the temporal pattern of taVNS effects with largest effect sizes during Days 2-4 (Cohen's d=0.50). This timing precedes the typical vasospasm window (Days 5-7), though the clinical benefit claim (C95) remains speculative without direct vasospasm outcome data.

results.result: Changes in SDNN (standard deviation of NN intervals) were not significantly different between treatment groups, though after adjusting for age, SDNN changes were significantly higher in the taVNS group.
results.evaluation: Claims C38 and C76 show that while unadjusted SDNN changes were not significant (p=0.479, Cohen's d=0.10), ANCOVA adjusting for age revealed significant differences. This suggests age is an important covariate affecting autonomic function changes after SAH.

results.result: Repetitive taVNS was associated with significantly lower peripheral perfusion index (PPI) changes and higher respiration rate changes compared to sham, with a negative correlation between PPI and respiration rate only in the taVNS group.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48, C83, C96 demonstrate statistically significant effects on PPI (p<0.01, Cohen's d=-0.49) and respiration rate (p=0.02, Cohen's d=0.37), with a significant negative correlation (r=-0.37, p<0.001) only in taVNS group. This suggests compensatory autonomic regulation to maintain cardiovascular homeostasis.

results.result: The relationship between high-frequency HRV power and respiration rate demonstrates that increased respiration rate in the taVNS group (>25 bpm) reduces high-frequency power, necessitating factor analysis to accurately measure parasympathetic activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 provide methodological validation showing that high-frequency power is confounded by respiration rate, with large effect size (Cohen's d=0.85) when comparing RR<25 vs >25 bpm. This justifies the factor analysis approach and explains the paradoxical lower high-frequency power in taVNS group at later phases.

results.result: Acute taVNS produced small increases in heart rate (within 0.5 SD of daily variation) and peripheral perfusion index, but did not significantly affect corrected QT interval, HRV, ICP, or blood pressure between treatment groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C49-C51, C61, C85-C86 show that acute effects differ from repetitive effects. While heart rate increased in taVNS group (p=0.03, Cohen's d=0.11), the magnitude was within normal daily variation and not significantly different between groups. Only PPI remained significant after Bonferroni correction.

results.result: Acute post-treatment elevation in heart rate was more pronounced in patients with improved clinical outcomes (mRS decrease >1 point), suggesting heart rate change may serve as a biomarker for identifying SAH patients likely to benefit from taVNS.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C52-C54, C62, C113, C117 show a significant interaction between treatment group and mRS change in predicting heart rate changes (Table 2), and post-hoc analysis shows patients with mRS improvement ≥2 had greater HR increases (p=0.02, Cohen's d=0.34). However, this is exploratory analysis requiring validation, and the mechanism remains unclear (C114).

results.result: Lower heart rate during treatment was associated with improved mRS scores across both treatment groups.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 shows a significant association between lower heart rate and improved mRS (p<0.01, Cohen's d=-0.54) using Mann-Whitney U test with adequate sample sizes (N=122 improved, N=98 not improved).

results.result: Acute taVNS produced small increases in PPI and blood pressure that remained within daily standard deviation, with no significant changes in ICP or respiration rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 show statistically significant acute increases in PPI (p<0.01, Cohen's d=0.19) and blood pressure (p=0.03, Cohen's d=0.22), though only PPI survived Bonferroni correction. The changes remained within normal daily variation, supporting safety.

results.result: taVNS treatment is safe in SAH patients without inducing adverse cardiovascular effects such as bradycardia or QT prolongation, with acute cardiovascular changes remaining within normal daily variations.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C59, C63, C90, C98, C115 synthesize the safety findings across multiple cardiovascular parameters. The absence of bradycardia, QT prolongation, and adverse blood pressure changes, combined with changes remaining within daily variation, support the safety conclusion.

results.result: Age negatively correlates with changes in heart rate, SDNN, and RMSSD but not QT intervals, with older individuals showing greater shift toward sympathetic predominance following SAH.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C75-C77 demonstrate through ANCOVA that age is a significant covariate affecting autonomic function changes. After age adjustment, treatment effects on RMSSD and SDNN became more pronounced, and lower HRV in older patients suggests greater sympathetic shift.

results.result: Higher HRV in the taVNS group aligns with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α and interleukin-6) reported in the primary outcomes of this trial.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 connects the HRV findings to the primary trial outcomes showing reduced inflammatory markers. This is supported by citations to the primary outcomes paper (Huguenard et al., 2024b) and established negative association between inflammation and HRV (Williams et al., 2019).

results.result: The observed acute increases in PPI following taVNS necessitate caution when considering treatment for patients in whom peripheral vasodilation is not desired.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 provides an appropriate cautionary recommendation based on the observed acute PPI increases. While the changes were within normal variation (C57), the consistent direction of effect warrants consideration for specific patient populations.

results.result: This study provides foundational data for future taVNS research in SAH patients, though systematic evaluation of stimulation parameters and mechanistic understanding of the heart rate biomarker are needed.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101, C114 appropriately identify future research directions. The study establishes safety and preliminary efficacy, but optimization of parameters (frequency, intensity, duration) and mechanistic validation of biomarkers require additional investigation.

results.result: The study has several limitations including not exploring less common cardiovascular metrics, high daily variability in HRV metrics, small sample sizes in later days, and complications from cardiac abnormalities common in SAH patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C109 transparently acknowledge study limitations. The justification for treating each day as independent (C103-C105) is reasonable given the clinical context, and the power calculation (C106) indicates 64 subjects per group would be needed for definitive day-by-day analysis.

results.result: Not all patients in the taVNS group showed clinical improvement, with differential response potentially influenced by anatomical variations in vagus nerve distribution at the outer ear.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 acknowledge individual variability in treatment response, supported by citation to similar findings in atrial fibrillation patients (Kulkarni et al., 2021). The anatomical variation hypothesis (C112) is speculative but plausible.

results.result: ECG signals were recorded using a 3-lead system at 500 Hz with appropriate filtering and preprocessing, including outlier removal and ectopic beat detection, to calculate cardiovascular metrics.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C140 describe the data acquisition and preprocessing methods in detail. The methods are standard for ECG analysis, with appropriate filtering (0.5 Hz high-pass, 60 Hz notch), validated QRS detection (Neurokit2), and reasonable outlier/ectopic beat criteria.

results.result: Exploratory factor analysis with Varimax rotation identified two factors underlying HRV metrics: overall HRV and parasympathetic activity, with variables normalized using z-scores based on individual daily means.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C147 describe appropriate factor analysis methodology. The use of Scree plot for factor selection, Minimum Residual Method for extraction, and Varimax rotation for interpretability are standard approaches. The normalization accounts for individual differences.

results.result: Statistical analyses used appropriate tests (t-tests for normal data, Mann-Whitney U for non-normal data) with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, equivalence testing for null findings, and power calculations for non-significant results.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C154 describe rigorous statistical methodology. The use of normality testing to select appropriate tests, Bonferroni correction (factor of 6 for cardiac metrics), equivalence testing with pre-specified margins, and power calculations for null findings demonstrate statistical rigor.

results.result: More than half of the patients were on vasopressor and inotropic drugs, complicating interpretation of blood pressure effects.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 acknowledges an important confounding factor in interpreting blood pressure results. This is a transparent limitation that appropriately qualifies the blood pressure findings.

results.result: The taVNS protocol was below perception threshold for all patients, with successful afferent vagal pathway activation potentially increasing arousal and heart rate.
results.evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by patient reports confirming imperceptibility. However, claim C88's mechanism (afferent activation increasing arousal) is speculative, supported only by citations without direct measurement of arousal or vagal activation in this study.

results.result: The study enrolled 24 SAH patients randomized to taVNS (N=11) or sham (N=13) treatment groups in a blinded randomized clinical trial. Patients received 20 minutes of stimulation twice daily during ICU stay, with taVNS delivered at 20 Hz frequency, 250 µs pulse width, and 0.4 mA intensity to the concha of the ear, while sham treatment involved ear clips on the earlobe without electrical current.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm the study design and methods. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'provide a solid set of data' and Reviewer 2 notes 'the methods are solid.' Reviewer 3 confirms that 'major concerns were largely addressed by the authors,' indicating acceptance of the study structure and methodology.

results.result: Repetitive taVNS did not significantly alter heart rate, blood pressure, or intracranial pressure (ICP) compared to sham treatment over the course of hospitalization. Equivalence testing confirmed that changes in these parameters were not significantly different between treatment groups.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support these safety findings. Reviewer 1 states the study 'supporting the safety of transcutaneous auricular vagal nerve stimulation on cardiovascular parameters.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the results showed that repetitive taVNS did not significantly alter heart rate, corrected QT interval, blood pressure, or intracranial pressure.' Reviewer 3 confirms the study 'concluded that taVNS treatment does not induce adverse cardiovascular effects.'

results.result: Changes in corrected QT interval from Day 1 were significantly lower in the taVNS group compared to sham (p<0.001, Cohen's d=-0.57), with large effect sizes after the early brain injury phase. The percentage of prolonged QT intervals was also significantly lower in the taVNS group (p<0.001, Cohen's d=-0.72), suggesting that taVNS reduces sympathetic overactivation and influences ventricular repolarization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as evidence of safety. Reviewer 3 explicitly states the study 'concluded that taVNS treatment does not induce adverse cardiovascular effects such as bradycardia or QT prolongation.' The QT interval findings are presented as supporting the safety profile rather than being questioned.

results.result: Repetitive taVNS significantly increased overall heart rate variability (HRV) and parasympathetic activity compared to sham treatment. Changes in RMSSD were significantly higher in the taVNS group (p=0.025, Cohen's d=0.42), with the largest effect on parasympathetic activity observed between Days 2-4 (Cohen's d=0.50). This suggests taVNS restores autonomic balance by enhancing parasympathetic tone following SAH.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these autonomic findings. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'suggests a promising effect on autonomic balance.' Reviewer 2 states 'it increased overall heart rate variability and parasympathetic activity after 5-10 days of treatment compared to the sham treatment.' These findings are presented as key contributions without critique.

results.result: Acutely, taVNS increased heart rate, blood pressure, and peripheral perfusion index (PPI) without affecting corrected QT interval, ICP, or HRV. The acute increase in heart rate in the taVNS group was statistically significant but small (Cohen's d=0.11) and remained within 0.5 standard deviations of daily heart rate. Only PPI remained significantly different after Bonferroni correction, and all acute changes remained within daily standard deviation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these acute findings as part of the safety profile. Reviewer 2 notes 'Acute taVNS led to an increase in heart rate, blood pressure, and peripheral perfusion index without affecting corrected QT interval, intracranial pressure, or heart rate variability.' The characterization of these changes as mild and within normal variation is not challenged.

results.result: The acute post-treatment elevation in heart rate was more pronounced in patients who experienced clinical improvement (decrease >1 point in modified Rankin Score). The slope between changes in heart rate and changes in mRS was significantly more negative for the taVNS group, suggesting that acute heart rate increase may serve as a biomarker for identifying SAH patients who are most likely to benefit from taVNS treatment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this biomarker finding. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'The mild acute increase in heart rate post-treatment could potentially serve as a biomarker for identifying SAH patients who may benefit more from taVNS therapy.' This finding is presented as a novel contribution without critique or requests for additional validation.

results.result: taVNS treatment did not induce adverse cardiovascular effects such as bradycardia or QT prolongation, supporting its development as a safe immunomodulatory treatment approach for SAH patients. The study substantiates the safety of treating SAH patients with taVNS and provides foundational data for future clinical translation.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly support the safety conclusions. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'provide a solid set of data supporting the safety.' Reviewer 3 notes 'This study contributes important information about the clinical utility of taVNS as a safe immunomodulatory treatment approach for SAH patients.' The safety conclusion is the primary finding that reviewers affirm.

results.result: PPI change was significantly lower in the taVNS group (p<0.01, Cohen's d=-0.49), while respiration rate change was significantly higher (p=0.02, Cohen's d=0.37). There was a significant negative correlation between changes in PPI and respiration rate only for the taVNS group (r=-0.37, p<0.001), suggesting autonomic system self-regulation to maintain cardiovascular homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings. Reviewer 2 notes the study 'monitored electrocardiogram (ECG) readings and vital signs' and found the 'presented data are convincing.' The PPI and respiration rate findings are part of the comprehensive cardiovascular assessment that reviewers accept.

results.result: The study confirmed that autonomic balance is shifted toward sympathetic dominance following SAH. Both parasympathetic activity factor and relative high-frequency power were higher in the taVNS group at the early phase (Days 2-4). The observed lower high-frequency power in the taVNS group at later phases was attributed to increased respiration rate, as normalized high-frequency power was higher when RR was <25 bpm compared to >25 bpm (Cohen's d=0.85).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these mechanistic findings. Reviewer 2 states 'The paper is overall well written, and the topic is of great interest. The methods are solid and the presented data are convincing.' The detailed HRV analysis and its interpretation are not questioned.

results.result: Age was negatively correlated with changes in heart rate, SDNN, and RMSSD from Day 1 but not with changes in QT intervals. After adjusting for age, RMSSD and SDNN changes were significantly higher, while QTc changes were significantly lower in the taVNS treatment group. Lower RMSSD and SDNN in older individuals suggest a greater shift toward sympathetic predominance following SAH.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about the age-adjusted analyses. Reviewer 3 notes that 'major concerns were largely addressed by the authors,' suggesting that any previous issues with covariates or confounders have been resolved. The age analysis is presented as supporting evidence without critique.

results.result: The finding that HRV was higher in the taVNS treatment group aligns with the primary outcomes of this clinical trial, which showed that taVNS treatment reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines including TNF-α and interleukin-6. This could lead to favorable clinical outcomes as lower HRV is associated with neurocardiogenic injury.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the connection between HRV findings and inflammatory outcomes. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'suggests a promising effect on autonomic balance,' which is consistent with the anti-inflammatory effects. The integration of cardiovascular and inflammatory findings is not challenged.

results.result: The observed acute increase in heart rate after taVNS treatment may serve as a biomarker for SAH patients who could derive greater benefit from this treatment. However, translating this finding into clinical practice will require further research to elucidate the mechanisms by which acute heart rate increase may predict outcomes, including its relationship with neurological evaluations, vasospasm, echocardiography, and inflammatory markers.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the biomarker finding, they implicitly acknowledge its preliminary nature. Reviewer 2 uses cautious language: 'could potentially serve as a biomarker,' indicating the speculative nature of this claim. The authors themselves acknowledge the need for 'further research to elucidate the mechanisms,' which reviewers do not dispute but also do not fully validate.

results.result: taVNS treatment mitigated sympathetic overactivation before the typical onset of cerebral vasospasm (5-7 days after SAH), potentially reducing the severity of this complication. Given that sympathetic predominance following SAH is implicated in increased risk of delayed cerebral vasospasm, the timing of taVNS effects may be clinically beneficial.
results.evaluation: This is a speculative mechanistic claim that reviewers do not explicitly validate. While reviewers accept the autonomic findings, they do not specifically comment on the vasospasm hypothesis. The claim uses cautious language ('potentially,' 'could') that indicates it is an inference rather than a demonstrated finding.

results.result: While acute cardiovascular changes were noted after taVNS, these changes were within normal daily variations, making them unlikely to pose a risk to the patient. However, the observed acute increases in PPI following taVNS necessitate caution when considering taVNS treatment for patients to whom peripheral vasodilation is not desired.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the safety assessment with appropriate caveats. Reviewer 1 affirms the study 'supporting the safety' while Reviewer 3 notes it 'contributes important information about the clinical utility of taVNS as a safe immunomodulatory treatment.' The cautionary note about PPI is presented as appropriate clinical consideration rather than a limitation.

results.result: The current study provides a basis for future preclinical and clinical studies of taVNS in SAH patients. A systematic evaluation of the relationship between stimulation parameters (frequency, intensity, duration) and taVNS's effects on the immune system and cardiovascular function is necessary to establish taVNS as an effective therapeutic option for SAH patients.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly support these recommendations for future research. Reviewer 3 notes that 'major concerns were largely addressed,' suggesting the study provides an adequate foundation. The call for parameter optimization is standard for early-phase trials and is not challenged.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on study design and methodology (C5, C27-C32, C118-C123). Both evaluations find the trial design, randomization, blinding procedures, and ethical approval well-documented and appropriate. All three peer reviewers explicitly affirm the methods are solid.

Complete agreement on cardiovascular safety findings (C6, C33-C34, C44-C45, C89). Both evaluations support that taVNS did not significantly alter heart rate, blood pressure, or intracranial pressure. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm the safety conclusions.

Full agreement on QT interval findings (C35-C37, C59, C73-C74). Both evaluations accept the statistically significant reductions in QTc changes as evidence supporting safety rather than raising concerns about QT prolongation.

Strong agreement on parasympathetic effects (C7, C39-C42, C60, C65-C66, C91, C116). Both evaluations affirm increased HRV and parasympathetic activity. OpenEval includes C8 in this result while peer review groups it separately, but both support the autonomic balance findings.

Partial overlap on temporal patterns. OpenEval R5 focuses on timing of effects (C8, C66, C68, C95) with largest effects on Days 2-4, while peer R4 addresses broader parasympathetic findings including C8 and C66. Both support the autonomic effects but emphasize different aspects.

Perfect agreement on PPI and respiration findings (C46-C48, C83, C96). Both evaluations accept the statistically significant effects and the compensatory autonomic regulation interpretation without challenge.

Strong agreement on methodological validation of HRV metrics (C67-C72). OpenEval emphasizes the confounding effect of respiration rate on high-frequency power, while peer review accepts the overall HRV analysis methods. Both support the factor analysis approach.

Strong agreement on acute effects (C9, C49-C51, C61, C85-C86). Both evaluations accept that acute heart rate increases were mild and within normal variation. Peer R5 also includes blood pressure findings (C55-C57) that OpenEval addresses separately in R12.

Agreement on heart rate as potential biomarker (C10, C52-C54, C62, C113, C117). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to exploratory nature requiring validation, while peer review explicitly SUPPORTS the finding. Both acknowledge it as a novel contribution, but OpenEval is more cautious about mechanistic clarity.

Agreement on acute PPI and blood pressure increases (C55-C58). Both evaluations accept these findings as part of the safety profile. OpenEval emphasizes that only PPI survived Bonferroni correction, while peer review presents both findings without this statistical nuance.

Complete agreement on overall safety conclusions (C11, C59, C63, C90, C115). Both evaluations strongly support the safety findings across multiple cardiovascular parameters. This is identified as the primary contribution by both evaluations.

Agreement on age as important covariate (C64, C75-C77). Both evaluations accept the age-adjusted ANCOVA findings showing treatment effects became more pronounced after adjustment. Peer review notes previous concerns were addressed.

Agreement on connection between HRV and inflammatory outcomes (C93). Both evaluations accept the link to reduced inflammatory markers from the primary trial. OpenEval cites supporting literature while peer review accepts the integration without challenge.

Agreement on cautionary recommendations (C99, C98). Both evaluations support the safety assessment with appropriate clinical caveats about PPI monitoring in specific patient populations. The cautionary note is presented as appropriate rather than a limitation.

Agreement on future research directions (C100-C101, C114). Both evaluations support the call for parameter optimization and mechanistic validation. Peer review implicitly accepts these as standard for early-phase trials.

Divergence on vasospasm hypothesis. OpenEval R5 includes C95 (clinical benefit claim regarding vasospasm) and rates it SUPPORTED but speculative. Peer R13 rates this claim as UNCERTAIN, noting reviewers did not explicitly validate the vasospasm mechanism despite accepting autonomic findings.

Slight divergence on mechanistic clarity. Both address C114 (need for mechanistic validation). OpenEval groups this with future research recommendations (SUPPORTED), while peer review treats it as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the preliminary nature of biomarker claims.

Minimal overlap on age-adjusted SDNN. OpenEval R6 focuses specifically on SDNN requiring age adjustment (C38, C76), while peer R10 addresses broader age effects (C75-C77). Both support age as an important covariate.

OpenEval identifies association between lower heart rate and improved mRS (C43) as SUPPORTED with adequate statistical evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this claim.

OpenEval evaluates study limitations (C102-C109) as appropriately acknowledged, including justification for treating days as independent and power calculations. Peer reviewers do not provide specific evaluation of these limitation claims.

OpenEval addresses individual variability in treatment response (C110-C112) as SUPPORTED with appropriate speculation about anatomical variation. Peer reviewers do not specifically evaluate these claims about response heterogeneity.

OpenEval evaluates ECG data acquisition and preprocessing methods (C129-C140) as SUPPORTED with standard approaches. Peer reviewers affirm methods are solid overall but do not provide specific evaluation of these technical details.

OpenEval assesses factor analysis methodology (C141-C147) as SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical techniques. Peer reviewers accept the overall analysis approach but do not specifically evaluate these methodological claims.

OpenEval evaluates statistical methodology (C148-C154) as SUPPORTED, noting rigorous use of normality testing, Bonferroni correction, and equivalence testing. Peer reviewers state methods are solid but do not provide detailed evaluation of these statistical procedures.

OpenEval identifies blood pressure confounding by antihypertensive medications (C84) as SUPPORTED transparent limitation. Peer reviewers do not specifically address this confounding factor in their evaluations.

OpenEval rates blinding effectiveness claims (C87-C88) as UNCERTAIN, with C87 supported by patient reports but C88's arousal mechanism speculative. Peer reviewers do not specifically evaluate these blinding-related claims.
